title: Chapter 6: What Theo Signed
content: Saturday the reading room opens at ten and Wren is on the third request slip by four minutes past, because the first two had a box she filled in wrong and the clerk handed them back without a word.
The slip wants a document number, a title, and a reason. The reason box is one line. She writes: family.
The clerk reads it and looks up over her glasses, which hang from a beaded chain, and says, "Family is not a reason. Reason means the record series."
"The release schedule," Wren says. "Permit B-4417. The gate."
The clerk writes B-4417 in the corner of the slip in a hand so small it looks printed. "Three folders at a time. Pencils only. No pens, no folders out of the room, no pages out of order."
"I know."
"Copy requests are ten cents a page and take twenty-four hours."
"I know that too."
The clerk puts the slip in a tray and goes away down the corridor, and her shoes make a sound on the linoleum like a metronome with a limp.

The reading room is on the second floor of the Annex, in what used to be the sorting floor. There are four tables, and one fan on a stand, and a window propped open with a book that somebody left here in 2019 because it is still propping the window. The mural from downstairs continues up here along the top of the wall, a band of painted river and painted men, and the paint is faded where the sun comes in.

There is a sign by the door under glass. It quotes the state public records act in two hundred words and ends with a sentence she has read eleven times now: public records shall be available for inspection and copying during posted hours.
She sits. The clock over the door has a second hand that moves in small jumps.

There is one other person in the room, a woman at the far table with a deed book open and a magnifying glass in her hand, who has been turning pages at the same rate since ten and has not once looked up. The radiator under the window knocks twice and stops.
At ten forty the clerk comes back with one folder and puts it on the table and does not let go of it until Wren has moved her pencil to the far side.
"Thirty-one pages," the clerk says. "Count them before you start and count them before you leave."
Wren counts them. She writes 31 in her notebook and the date, and then she takes the pages one at a time and writes what each one is.

Page 1, application for a water obstruction permit, District 4, Kettler Gate, filed 2 February 2026. Page 2, the drawing, a cross section of the gate with the gatesill and the stilling basin. Pages 3 through 9, correspondence, nine letters, all of them short. Pages 10 through 13, a hydrology memo with two tables of flow rates.
Pages 14 through 18 are the study.

It has a title page with a rule under the title and a stamp in the corner that says DISTRICT 4 COPY. SILT CLEARANCE EFFICACY STUDY, KETTLER GATE, MILE 12, SABLE RIVER. Prepared for the Basin Authority, District 4. Prepared by T. Marsh, P.E.
She looks at the name for a while. Then she reads the study.

Page 15 is the method. Five sampling transects at Mile 12 and two below the gate at Mile 9, bed load measured by a sampler she has seen hanging in the shed at the landing, a cylinder on a cable that she has hauled up full of gravel a hundred times without knowing what it was for.

She did not know the phrase bed load then. She knows what it sounds like. When the gate lets go, the gravel moves down the channel and hits the piling at the landing and the whole deck rings like a struck pipe, and she has heard that sound at two in the morning with her hand on the railing and no idea in the world what it meant.
Page 16 is the findings. There is a graph with a curve on it that rises steeply and then flattens, and under the graph there is a paragraph.
She reads the paragraph twice.

A pulse of ninety seconds duration produces a shear front sufficient to mobilize the deposited bed load and carry it below Mile 9. A slower rise of 180 seconds or greater would not clear the silt and would require a second release within the same season, which the permit does not allow.
She reads it a third time. The fan turns on its stand and moves the air across the table and the corner of page 16 lifts and settles.

Ninety seconds. She has been in the water in ninety seconds. She knows exactly how far a river can come in ninety seconds, because she has stood on the levee and watched it come, and because on the twelfth of September she was standing on the deck with her hand on the rail when the cable went slack.
Page 17 is the recommendation, and it is written in the flat voice of a man doing his job.

Recommendation 4.2: the district should schedule the third release of the 2026 season at the maximum permitted rate for the minimum effective duration. Recommend commencement at 21:45, at the close of the recreational day, when the reach below Mile 9 is typically clear of anglers.

She stops at that. She reads it again to be sure of it. Close of the recreational day. Typically clear of anglers. He has thought about who would be on the water, and he has decided that a quarter to ten at night is when the water is empty.
Page 18 is the signature block.
T. Marsh, P.E. State license 44-2019-0871. 14 May 2026.

She knows the handwriting. She has known it since a grocery list on the back of a survey sheet, milk and coffee and a bag of ice, with the eggs added at the bottom in a different pen because he had already put his coat on. The seven in the date has a crossbar through it. The g in Marsh closes at the bottom like a loop of rope. He signs his name the way he wrote that list, fast, with the last letter running off the line.
She puts her finger on the signature and does not press.
"Miss," the clerk says. She is standing at the end of the table. "No touching."
Wren takes her finger back.
At eleven twenty she asks for the second folder, the release schedule table for the permit year, and the clerk brings it in eight minutes, and this one is four pages and mostly a grid.
Release 1 of 4, 18 April. Release 2 of 4, 7 June. Release 3 of 4, 12 September. Release 4 of 4, date pending.
Release 3 has a column for the estimated effect at the crossing.
Estimated commencement 21:45. Duration 90 seconds. Estimated stage rise at Mile 9: six feet one inch. Estimated duration above bankfull: four minutes.

Six feet one inch. In 1908 somebody painted a nine on a hull. In 1908 somebody built a landing at Mile 9 with three feet of freeboard and a ramp that goes down to the gravel. She has been tying a boat to that landing since she was eleven years old, and she has never once seen the water come over the top of the piling, and on the twelfth of September it came over the top of the piling and kept going.
She copies the grid into her notebook in pencil, every number, and then she takes her phone out of her coat.
"No photographs," the clerk says. She says it before the phone is out of the pocket, as if she has been watching for it.
"The sign says inspection and copying."
"Copying is ten cents a page and twenty-four hours."

"Copying is what I asked for," Wren says. "You told me twenty-four hours. I don't have twenty-four hours. I have a Saturday." She turns the phone over in her hand. "Show me the rule that says I can't take a picture of a public record."
The clerk's mouth goes small.

"If it's written down, I'll put the phone away," Wren says. "I'll wait the twenty-four hours and I'll pay the three dollars and ten cents and I'll come back Monday. But if it isn't written down, I'm going to photograph all thirty-one pages right now, in front of you, and put the folder back in the same order, and count it while you watch."
The clerk stands there. The fan turns. Downstairs a door opens and closes.
"There's no rule," the clerk says.
"No," Wren says. "There isn't."

She photographs the pages. It takes six minutes and the clerk watches every second of it with her arms folded, and when Wren is done she squares the edges of the folder and counts the pages out loud, thirty-one, and hands it back.

Then she takes three dollars and ten cents out of her pocket in coins and puts them on the table, because she asked for copies and she is not going to be a person who asked for copies and did not pay for them.
The clerk looks at the coins. "You don't have to."
"I do," Wren says. "It's the only receipt I'll get."
She picks up her pencil and writes 3.10 in the notebook and circles it, and then she says, "I'd like the 2025 permit year. Same series."
The clerk goes to the card index by the door and runs a finger down the drawer and stops.
"That one's out," she says.
"Out where."
"Signed out." She turns the card around. There is a date in the corner in the same small printed hand. "To the district office. Director's office."
Wren looks at the card. It has been out since March.
"When does it come back."
"It doesn't," the clerk says. "They don't bring them back. They keep them and we make a new card that says retained."
"Retained by who."
"By them," the clerk says, and closes the drawer, and Wren understands that this is not a woman being difficult. This is a woman telling her the shape of the building.

She goes down the stairs into the lobby where the brass boxes are, and past the mural of men with shovels, and out through the double doors onto Third Street, where the rain has stopped and the sidewalk is steaming and the crack in the asphalt is full of water.
She sits on the top step with the phone in both hands and opens the first photograph and pinches it until the graph fills the screen.
21:45. Ninety seconds. Six feet one inch.

She remembers the clock on the ferry, the brass one screwed to the wheelhouse wall that ran four minutes fast all summer and that her grandfather would not let her fix. She remembers looking at it when the deck went out from under her feet. 9:47.
She sits on the step and does the arithmetic that is not arithmetic.
He wrote 21:45 in May, in a room in Columbus, with a graph in front of him and a license number after his name, and the water came at 9:47.
Two minutes. She looks at the street and thinks about how long two minutes is, and how much of it a man can spend in the water.
highlight: In the reading room Wren finds Theo's own survey recommending the release that killed her grandfather.
